title: One value, four printf conversions
request: Teach me how printf shows the same int with %d, %u, %f and %c, as all six media.

diagnostics.clang:
ub.c:5:20: warning: format specifies type 'double' but the argument has type 'int' [-Wformat]
    5 |     printf("%f\n", a);
      |             ~~     ^
      |             %d
1 warning generated.
diagnostics.gcc-16:
ub.c: In function 'main':
ub.c:5:14: warning: format '%f' expects argument of type 'double', but argument 2 has type 'int' [-Wformat=]
    5 |     printf("%f\n", a);
      |             ~^     ~
      |              |     |
      |              |     int
      |              double
      |             %d

claims.text: The program stores 66 in the int a.
66 fits in the low byte of a. Its bits are 01000010, which is 0x42 in hex.
claims.justification: 66 = 64 + 2 = 2^6 + 2^1, so bits 6 and 1 are set: 01000010. Lines 7-8 take bit 7-i with (a >> (7 - i)) & 1, which for a nonnegative a is bit 7-i of the value (6.5.7p5). Line 10 prints the value with %#x, which prefixes 0x (7.21.6.1p6). The run printed 01000010 and 0x42.

sources.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 (C17), working draft N2176
sources.quote: The result of E1 >> E2 is E1 right-shifted E2 bit positions. If E1 has an unsigned type or if E1 has a signed type and a nonnegative value, the value of the result is the integral part of the quotient of E1 / 2E2.

claims.text: %d prints an int as a signed decimal number, so it prints 66.
claims.justification: 7.21.6.1p8, conversion d: the int argument is converted to signed decimal. a is 66; the run printed 66 on line 3.

sources.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 (C17), working draft N2176
sources.quote: The int argument is converted to signed decimal in the style [−]dddd.

claims.text: (unsigned)a converts 66 to unsigned int. 66 fits there, so the value stays 66 and %u prints 66.
claims.justification: 6.3.1.3p1: a value representable in the new integer type is unchanged; 66 is representable in unsigned int. %u converts an unsigned int to unsigned decimal (7.21.6.1p8). The run printed 66 on line 4.

sources.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 (C17), working draft N2176
sources.quote: When a value with integer type is converted to another integer type other than _Bool, if the value can be represented by the new type, it is unchanged.

claims.text: (double)a converts the value 66 to the double 66.0. On this machine, where double is IEC 60559 binary64, that double's bits are 0x4050800000000000, not the bits of a.
claims.justification: 6.3.1.4p2: an integer value exactly representable in the floating type is unchanged, so the result is 66.0. On this platform double is IEC 60559 binary64 (Annex F): 66 = 1.03125 x 2^6, sign 0, biased exponent 1023 + 6 = 1029 = 0x405, fraction 0.03125 = 2^-5, giving 0x4050800000000000. Lines 15-18 copy the double's bytes into an unsigned long long with memcpy and print them; the run printed 0x4050800000000000, while a's own value is 0x42.

sources.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 (C17), working draft N2176
sources.quote: When a value of integer type is converted to a real floating type, if the value being converted can be represented exactly in the new type, it is unchanged.

sources.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 (C17), working draft N2176
sources.quote: The double type matches the IEC 60559 double format.

claims.text: %f prints a double with six digits after the decimal point when no precision is given, so it prints 66.000000.
claims.justification: 7.21.6.1p8, conversion f: style [−]ddd.ddd with precision digits after the point; a missing precision is taken as 6. The argument is the double 66.0; the run printed 66.000000 on line 5.

sources.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 (C17), working draft N2176
sources.quote: A double argument representing a floating-point number is converted to decimal notation in the style [−]ddd.ddd, where the number of digits after the decimal-point character is equal to the precision specification. If the precision is missing, it is taken as 6

claims.text: %c converts the int 66 to unsigned char and writes that character. In ASCII, code 66 is B.
claims.justification: 7.21.6.1p8, conversion c without l: the int argument is converted to an unsigned char and the resulting character is written. The execution character set here is ASCII (macOS), where 66 is 'B'. The run printed B on line 6.

sources.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 (C17), working draft N2176
sources.quote: If no l length modifier is present, the int argument is converted to an unsigned char, and the resulting character is written.

claims.text: printf does not reinterpret the bits of a for %f. It receives the double that (double)a made.
claims.justification: The argument expression on line 13 is (double)a, of type double, so the value passed through the ellipsis is the double 66.0 (6.5.2.2p7: trailing arguments get the default argument promotions; a double stays a double). %f converts that double argument (7.21.6.1p8). The int's bits are never what %f reads in views.c.

sources.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 (C17), working draft N2176
sources.quote: The ellipsis notation in a function prototype declarator causes argument type conversion to stop after the last declared parameter. The default argument promotions are performed on trailing arguments.

claims.text: Without the cast, printf("%f\n", a) passes an int where %f needs a double, and the behaviour is undefined.
claims.justification: 7.21.6.1p9: if any argument is not the correct type for its conversion specification, the behavior is undefined. %f requires a double; a is an int. clang warns about ub.c line 5 with -Wformat.

sources.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 (C17), working draft N2176
sources.quote: If any argument is not the correct type for the corresponding conversion specification, the behavior is undefined.

claims.text: So ub.c is compiled for its warning and never run.
claims.justification: lesson.json marks ub.c ub: true and run: false; ptk compiles it, records the warning, and never runs it, so no output of it is shown.

claims.text: Pause here and predict the output before you go on.
claims.justification: An instruction to the learner; it states nothing about C.

claims.text: %d and %c get the int a, and %u gets the unsigned int 66, which has the same bits. %f gets a new value, the double 66.0, whose bits differ.
claims.justification: Line 11 passes a to %d and line 14 passes a to %c (which converts it to unsigned char inside printf, 7.21.6.1p8). Line 12 passes (unsigned)a: 66 is representable in unsigned int, so the value is unchanged (6.3.1.3p1), and a nonnegative value has the same representation in a signed type and its unsigned type (6.2.5p9). Line 13 passes (double)a, the double 66.0 (6.3.1.4p2), whose bits on this binary64 machine are 0x4050800000000000 (run line 7), not 0x42.

sources.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 (C17), working draft N2176
sources.quote: The range of nonnegative values of a signed integer type is a subrange of the corresponding unsigned integer type, and the representation of the same value in each type is the same.

misconceptions.statement: printf reinterprets the same bits for %f, so it reads the bits of a as a double.
%f prints a whole number with no decimal places when the value is whole.

trace.label: a holds 66: its low byte is 01000010
(double)a makes a new double; %f prints it

storyboard.title: The int and its low byte

narration.text: The program stores 66 in the integer variable a.
66 fits in the low byte of a. Its bits are 0 1 0 0 0 0 1 0, which is hex 42.
Pause here and predict the output before you go on.

storyboard.title: The cast makes a new double

narration.text: The cast to double converts the value 66 to the double 66.0. On this machine, that double's bits are not the bits of a.
Percent f prints a double with 6 digits after the decimal point when no precision is given, so it prints 66 followed by a point and six zeros.
Percent d prints an int as a signed decimal number, so it prints 66.
The cast to unsigned converts 66 to an unsigned int. 66 fits there, so the value stays 66, and percent u, too, prints 66.
Percent c converts the int 66 to an unsigned char, and writes that character. In ASCII, code 66 is B.
printf does not reinterpret the bits of a for percent f. It receives the double that the cast made.
Without the cast, passing a to percent f gives printf an int where it needs a double, and the behaviour is undefined.
So the file ub dot c is compiled for its warning, and never run.
Percent d and percent c get the int a, and percent u gets the unsigned int 66, which has the same bits. Percent f gets a new value, the double 66.0, whose bits differ.
